Professor Hinshaw is a very enthusiastic teacher and an untiring worker, laboring for the upbuilding of the Seminary, his work being thorough and exhaustive. He prepares himself thoroughly in the work and he seems tireless in his efforts. He has adopted the branches of study not only beneficial but attractive and pleasant, and is continually on the alert to promote the usefulness of the school. He is a pleasant gentlemen, and is also a factor in advancing culture and intellectuality in the community in which it is located.

Professor Hinshaw was united in marriage to Miss Mary Hianott, a teacher of Bloomfield who had educated in Victoria College in that State. Both the Professor and his wife are consistent members of the Cumberland Presbyterian Church, whose lives together have been an exemplification of its teachings, an example which has been held up before the pupils of the Seminary. He is a very prominent and exemplary member of the Masonic Lodge. He is a musician of ability, having completed his music under the second degree in the Scottish Rite and is also a noble of the Mystic Shrine. . . . His home life is one of the models of broad culture, refined intercourse, charming conversation—all that is of domestic companionship and culture and all that is good and fine in social life.

Mr. Hinshaw remained in his position as superintendent of the Bloomfield Seminary for eighteen years, up to the close of the tribal government, marrying and remaining in the Chickasaw territory, married Mrs. Henry Naylor, and continued in educational work up to the time of his death. Later he married for the second time and after that was connected with the Southeastern State Normal School at Durant, and became one of its teachers. He was a close friend of Governor Johnston, the last chief of the Chickasaw Nation. Mr. Hinshaw died in Oklahoma City, June 27, 1920, and was buried in Collinsville, Texas, where his widow still lives.
